there was no genetic variation in inducer of resistance to herbivores in a natural population, but there was genetic variation in the levels of constitutive and inducible resistance to herbivore damage.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is genetic variation in trypsin inhibitors in B. rapa and that this variation is associated with variation in resistance to herbivores, but that this variation is not necessarily associated with the inducibility of trypsin inhibitor production by herbivore feeding.
there are significant genetic correlations between induced resistance and constitutive resistance to herbivores in this species, but that the nature of these correlations remains unclear.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a lack of genetic variation in glucosinolase and trypsin inhibitors and that the induction of these defenses is a nonvariable trait in the population studied.
the inducibility of resistance in this species is highly plastic but the genetic variation in inducer and inducible resistance is limited.
the genetic architecture of resistance is complex and that the genetic architecture is likely to be different for different types of resistance and different species.
The main takeaway from our work is that

genetic variation in inducer- and herbivore-specific defenses can be studied in a population by growing plants in pairs, exposing only one plant to herbivory and then comparing the responses of the control and induced plants in a bioassay.

the study of the genetic basis of inducibility of plant defenses is complicated because of the confounding effects of genetic variation in the constitutive levels of defenses and genetic variation in the response to herbivory.
the genetic variation in constitutive and induced levels of glucosinalotes and trypsin inhibitors in B. rapa is not consistent with the predictions of the optimal defense theory.
